position: predicative only — after a verb: *he was stark naked*, not *a stark naked man*
contrast: *Stark* as an intensifier lives in only a couple of fixed phrases: *stark naked*, *stark raving mad*. On its own *stark* means bare or harsh: *a stark white room*.

senses.gloss: Wearing no clothes at all.
senses.ru: совершенно голый, в чём мать родила
examples: He ran out of the sauna *stark naked*.
The baby was *stark naked* and perfectly happy about it.
I opened the door and there he stood, *stark naked*.

position: attributive only — before a noun: *a starlit night*

senses.gloss: Lit only by the light of the stars.
examples: They walked home along a *starlit* beach.
We ate dinner outside on a warm, *starlit* evening.
The *starlit* sky over the desert was unbelievable.

senses.gloss: Full of stars, or showing a lot of stars.
examples: It was a cold, *starry* night in late October.
The sky gets *starrier* the farther you drive from the city.
Out in the desert the sky was *starry* from one horizon to the other.

senses.gloss: So full of hope and admiration that you cannot see the problems.
examples: He arrived in Los Angeles *starry-eyed* and broke.
She is still *starry-eyed* about the new job.
A few *starry-eyed* fans waited outside the hotel all night.

position: attributive only — before a noun: *a starting salary*

senses.gloss: At the beginning of something, before anything changes.
examples: The *starting* salary is fifty thousand a year.
Let's take her question as our *starting* point.
The *starting* price for the base model is under thirty thousand.

senses.gloss: In sports: chosen to play from the first minute, not from the bench.
examples: He is the *starting* quarterback this season.
She made the *starting* lineup as a freshman.

contrast: *startled* is the person, *startling* is the thing that does it: *a startled cat*, *a startling noise*.

senses.gloss: Suddenly surprised or a little frightened by something you did not expect.
examples: She looked *startled* when I said her name.
A *startled* deer jumped out of the ditch.
He was even *more startled* by the news than I was.

contrast: The *-ing* form is the thing; the *-ed* form is the person: *a startling result*, *a startled reader*.

senses.gloss: So surprising that it makes you stop short.
examples: The report contains some *startling* numbers.
There is a *startling* resemblance between the two brothers.
The results were *more startling* than anyone had expected.

senses.gloss: Not given enough of something it badly needs.
examples: Rural hospitals have been *starved* of money for years.
Those kids are *starved* for attention.
A plant *starved* of light will never flower.

senses.gloss: Informal: extremely hungry.
examples: I'm absolutely *starved* — when is dinner?
We were *starved* by the time we got home.

senses.gloss: Owned and run by the government rather than by private owners.
examples: *State-controlled* television carried the speech live.
Most of the oil industry there is *state-controlled*.
The paper is *state-controlled*, so nobody believes a word of it.

position: attributive only — before a noun: *the stated reason*

senses.gloss: Given officially as the reason or the aim — often with a hint that the real one is different.
examples: Her *stated* reason for leaving was the commute.
The *stated* goal of the program is to cut emissions in half.
He never goes beyond the company's *stated* policy.

senses.gloss: Having no country that recognizes you as a citizen.
examples: Thousands of children are born *stateless* every year.
A *stateless* person cannot get a passport.
The treaty is meant to protect *stateless* refugees.

contrast: *Stately* ends in *-ly* but is an adjective: *a stately home*, never *he walked stately*.

senses.gloss: Large, dignified and impressive, in a slow and formal way.
examples: They live in a *stately* old house on the hill.
The procession moved at a *stately* pace.
The hotel lobby is *stately* but a little cold.

senses.gloss: Covering a whole US state.
examples: The ban is now *statewide*.
She won the *statewide* election by nine points.
There is a *statewide* shortage of math teachers.

senses.gloss: Not moving and not changing.
examples: Prices have stayed *static* since the spring.
The design is completely *static* — nothing on the page moves.
The population of the town is more or less *static*.

senses.gloss: Of electricity that builds up on a surface instead of flowing.
examples: *Static* electricity made her hair stand straight up.
The carpet gives me a *static* shock every winter.

contrast: *stationary* (not moving) and *stationery* (paper and envelopes, a noun) sound the same: *a stationary car*, *a box of stationery*.

senses.gloss: Standing still; not moving.
examples: The truck hit a *stationary* car at the light.
Traffic was *stationary* for almost an hour.
She rides a *stationary* bike at the gym every morning.

position: attributive only — before a noun: *statistical evidence*

senses.gloss: Having to do with numbers collected and analyzed to show a pattern.
examples: There is no *statistical* evidence for that claim.
The paper includes a full *statistical* analysis of the survey.
A *statistical* error of two percent is normal here.

senses.gloss: Of a woman: tall, well-built and dignified, like a statue.
examples: A *statuesque* woman in a red dress crossed the lobby.
She is *statuesque* and towers over everyone in the photo.
The actress looked *statuesque* on the red carpet.

position: attributive only — before a noun: *a statutory limit*

senses.gloss: Required or fixed by a written law.
examples: There is a *statutory* limit on how much they can charge.
Employers have to give the *statutory* minimum notice.
Missing the deadline carries a *statutory* penalty.

senses.gloss: Very loyal and firm in supporting a person, a party or a belief.
examples: She is a *staunch* supporter of the public library.
He became one of her *staunchest* defenders.
The senator is a *staunch* opponent of the tax.

position: attributive only — before a noun: *a stay-at-home dad*
form: compound — a whole phrase used as one adjective

senses.gloss: Staying at home to raise the children instead of working outside the house.
senses.ru: сидящий дома с детьми, неработающий (о родителе)
examples: He has been a *stay-at-home* dad for six years.
Her mother was a *stay-at-home* mom in the seventies.
The article compares *stay-at-home* and working parents.

senses.gloss: Staying loyal or firm and refusing to change, whatever happens.
examples: She has been a *steadfast* friend for thirty years.
He was *steadfast* in his refusal to sign.
Their support for the team stayed *steadfast* through a terrible season.

senses.gloss: Firm and not shaking or moving.
examples: Hold the ladder *steady* while I climb up.
A surgeon needs *steady* hands.
His voice was *steadier* than I expected.

senses.gloss: Going on at the same rate without stopping or jumping around.
examples: There has been a *steady* rise in rents since 2020.
We drove at a *steady* sixty miles an hour.
A *steady* rain fell all afternoon.

senses.gloss: Regular and dependable, so you can count on it.
examples: He finally found a *steady* job with benefits.
She has a *steady* boyfriend now.

senses.gloss: Moving or done quietly and secretly so that nobody notices.
examples: The cat made a *stealthy* move toward the bird.
It was a *stealthy* attempt to change the rules without a vote.
Cats are *stealthier* than any dog will ever be.

senses.gloss: Driven by the pressure of steam.
examples: The museum has a working *steam-powered* locomotive.
Early factories were *steam-powered*.
He restores *steam-powered* tractors as a hobby.

senses.gloss: Cooked over boiling water rather than in it.
examples: We had rice and *steamed* broccoli.
The fish comes *steamed*, with ginger and scallions.

senses.gloss: Informal: angry and showing it.
examples: He was pretty *steamed* about the delay.
Don't get *steamed* — it was an honest mistake.

senses.gloss: So hot that steam is rising from it.
examples: She set a *steaming* bowl of soup in front of me.
The horses stood *steaming* in the cold air.
He carried in two *steaming* mugs of coffee.

senses.gloss: Hot and wet with steam or humid air.
examples: The bathroom was *steamy* after his shower.
August in Houston is hot and *steamy*.
It was the *steamiest* week of the summer.

senses.gloss: Informal: full of sexual excitement.
examples: The book has a few *steamy* scenes.
They had a *steamy* affair one summer.

position: attributive only — before a noun: *a steely stare*

senses.gloss: Hard, cold and completely determined.
examples: She gave him a *steely* stare and said nothing.
Behind the smile there is *steely* determination.

senses.gloss: Of the cold gray-blue color of steel.
examples: He has *steely* gray eyes.
The lake was a flat *steely* blue that morning.

senses.gloss: Rising or falling sharply, at a big angle.
examples: The path up to the lake is short but *steep*.
This is the *steepest* street in the city.
There was a *steep* drop on the other side of the wall.

senses.gloss: Of a rise or fall in numbers: large and fast.
examples: The company reported a *steep* drop in sales.
There has been a *steep* rise in the cost of insurance.

senses.gloss: Informal, of a price: much higher than it should be.
examples: Forty dollars for parking seems a little *steep*.
The rent is *steep*, but the place is beautiful.

senses.gloss: Excellent; far better than the usual standard.
examples: She gave a *stellar* performance in the second act.
His grades were not exactly *stellar* that semester.

senses.gloss: Technical: having to do with stars.
examples: The telescope measures *stellar* distances.
A supernova is the end of a *stellar* life cycle.

position: attributive only — before a noun: *step-by-step instructions*
form: compound — a whole phrase used as one adjective
contrast: Before a noun it is hyphenated; after a verb it becomes the adverb phrase *step by step*: *a step-by-step guide*, but *we did it step by step*.

senses.gloss: Explained or done one stage at a time, in order.
examples: The manual has *step-by-step* instructions with pictures.
She wrote a *step-by-step* guide for new hires.
It is a *step-by-step* process, and you cannot skip ahead.

position: attributive only — before a noun: *stereo sound*
contrast: The thing in your living room is a noun: *I bought a new stereo*. Only the sound sense is an adjective: *a stereo recording*.

senses.gloss: Of sound: coming from two separate channels, so it seems to spread out in space.
examples: The band's first *stereo* recording came out in 1963.
Older television sets did not have *stereo* sound.
Headphones give you the full *stereo* effect.

senses.gloss: Shown in a fixed, oversimplified way that ignores what people are really like.
examples: The movie is full of *stereotyped* characters.
Textbooks used to give a very *stereotyped* picture of family life.
Her role was *stereotyped* and gave her nothing to do.

senses.gloss: Matching a tired, oversimplified idea of what a group or thing is like.
examples: He is the *stereotypical* absent-minded professor.
The ad plays on *stereotypical* ideas about teenagers.
Nothing about her job is *stereotypical* for an engineer.

senses.gloss: Completely free of germs.
examples: Cover the cut with a *sterile* bandage.
The needles come in *sterile* packaging.
Operating rooms have to be kept *sterile*.

senses.gloss: Unable to produce children, young or crops.
examples: The treatment can leave a patient *sterile*.
Years of salt water left the soil *sterile*.

senses.gloss: Lacking warmth, life or new ideas.
examples: The lobby is clean but *sterile*, like a dentist's office.
The debate has become *sterile* — nobody learns anything.

contrast: American spelling is *sterilized*; British books print *sterilised*.

senses.gloss: Cleaned of all germs, usually with heat or chemicals.
examples: Use *sterilized* jars for the jam.
Every instrument on the tray has been *sterilized*.

senses.gloss: Of an animal or person: operated on so that they cannot have young.
examples: All the cats at the shelter are *sterilized* before adoption.
The dog was *sterilized* at six months.

position: attributive only — before a noun: *sterling work*

senses.gloss: Excellent, and deserving real praise.
examples: She did a *sterling* job of organizing the whole trip.
He has a reputation for *sterling* honesty.

senses.gloss: Of silver: of the standard high quality, 92.5 percent pure.
examples: The spoons are *sterling* silver, not plate.
Look for a *sterling* mark on the back.

senses.gloss: Serious and strict, and not ready to forgive.
examples: Our coach was *stern* but fair.
She gave the boys a *stern* look over her glasses.
The judge had a *sterner* warning for the second driver.

senses.gloss: Cooked slowly in liquid in a covered pot.
examples: We had *stewed* tomatoes with the chicken.
She serves *stewed* apples over oatmeal.
The beef is *stewed* for three hours until it falls apart.

position: attributive only — before a noun: *stick-on labels*

senses.gloss: Made with glue on the back so you can just press it into place.
examples: I put *stick-on* labels on all the storage bins.
The kids covered the window with *stick-on* stars.
You can buy *stick-on* hooks that hold a few pounds.

senses.gloss: Covered with something that glues itself to whatever it touches.
examples: The kids' hands were *sticky* with candy.
Use a *sticky* note to mark the page.
The dough gets *stickier* if you add more water.

senses.gloss: Of weather: hot and damp in an uncomfortable way.
examples: It was a *sticky* afternoon with no wind at all.
July here is hot and *sticky*.

senses.gloss: Informal: awkward and difficult to get out of.
examples: The question about money got a little *sticky*.
He got himself into a *sticky* situation with his landlord.

senses.gloss: Hard and difficult to bend or move.
examples: The card is printed on *stiff* paper.
This drawer is *stiff* — you have to pull hard.
Beat the egg whites until they are *stiff*.

senses.gloss: Of a body part: sore and hard to move.
examples: I woke up with a *stiff* neck.
My legs were *stiffer* the second day than the first.

senses.gloss: Formal and unfriendly in the way someone behaves.
examples: He gave a *stiff* little bow and left.
The conversation stayed polite but *stiff*.

senses.gloss: Stronger or more severe than usual.
examples: There is *stiff* competition for those jobs.
He poured himself a *stiff* drink.
A *stiff* breeze came off the water.

position: attributive only — before a noun: *a stifled laugh*

senses.gloss: Held back so that it is barely heard or never comes out.
examples: There was a *stifled* laugh from the back row.
She answered with a *stifled* yawn.
The report describes years of *stifled* dissent.

senses.gloss: So hot and airless that it is hard to breathe.
examples: The heat in the attic was *stifling*.
We sat through a *stifling* August afternoon with no fan.

senses.gloss: So controlling that it leaves no room to think or act freely.
examples: She left a *stifling* job where nobody could question anything.
He found small-town life *stifling*.

contrast: Most of the time *still* is an adverb (*She is still here*, *Are you still mad?*). The adjective means not moving: *Sit still*, *the still water*.

senses.gloss: Not moving at all.
examples: Hold *still* while I take the picture.
The water was so *still* you could see every cloud in it.
The lake is *stiller* at dawn than at any other hour.

senses.gloss: Quiet and calm, with nothing stirring.
examples: It was a warm, *still* evening in June.
The house went completely *still* after they left.

senses.gloss: Of a drink: without bubbles.
examples: Would you like sparkling or *still* water?
They only sell *still* water at that counter.

senses.gloss: Born dead.
examples: Their first child was *stillborn*.
The clinic keeps records of *stillborn* births.

senses.gloss: Of a plan or idea: failing before it ever gets going.
examples: The peace plan was *stillborn* — nobody would sign it.
His campaign was *stillborn* by the end of January.

senses.gloss: Of speech or writing: stiff and unnatural, as if nobody really talks that way.
examples: The dialogue in the film is painfully *stilted*.
We had a *stilted* conversation about the weather.
His English is correct but *stilted*.

senses.gloss: Making you interested and full of new ideas.
examples: It was the most *stimulating* class I took all year.
She finds the work *stimulating* even after ten years.

senses.gloss: Making the body or mind more active.
examples: Coffee has a *stimulating* effect that lasts a few hours.
Cold water on your face is surprisingly *stimulating*.

position: attributive only — before a noun: *a stinging pain*

senses.gloss: Causing a sharp burning pain on the skin.
examples: The soap left a *stinging* sensation in my eyes.
A *stinging* wind blew snow into our faces.

senses.gloss: Of words: sharp and meant to hurt.
examples: The review was a *stinging* attack on the whole company.
She had a *stinging* reply ready for him.

senses.gloss: Unwilling to spend or give, even when there is plenty.
examples: He is famously *stingy* with tips.
Don't be *stingy* — put more cheese on it.
The new boss is *stingier* about overtime than the last one.

senses.gloss: Smelling very bad.
examples: A *stinking* pile of garbage sat by the curb.
The whole basement was damp and *stinking*.

senses.gloss: Informal, before a noun: used to show anger or disgust at something.
examples: I don't want your *stinking* money.
He wouldn't move his *stinking* car out of the driveway.

senses.gloss: Informal: smelling bad — the everyday word, common with kids.
examples: Take off those *stinky* socks before you come in.
The dog rolled in something *stinky* again.
This is the *stinkiest* cheese in the store.

senses.gloss: Making people feel strong emotion, usually pride or excitement.
examples: She gave a *stirring* speech at the memorial.
The film ends with a *stirring* piece of music.
His account of the rescue was *stirring*.

position: attributive only — before a noun: *a stock answer*
contrast: *Stock* is much more often a noun (*shares of stock*, *chicken stock*). As an adjective it only goes before a noun and means standard or routine.

senses.gloss: Used so often that it is no longer fresh; ready-made.
examples: He gave the *stock* answer about needing more data.
The speech was full of *stock* phrases.

senses.gloss: Of a standard kind that a store or factory keeps ready.
examples: The shelves come in four *stock* sizes.
It is a *stock* model with no extras.

position: predicative only — after a verb like *stand*, *sit* or *be*

senses.gloss: Completely motionless.
examples: The deer stood *stock-still* in the middle of the road.
He sat *stock-still* until the noise stopped.
She was *stock-still*, listening for the car.

position: both — usually with an adverb: *well stocked*, *fully stocked*

senses.gloss: Filled with a supply of goods or food.
examples: The pantry is fully *stocked* for the week.
It is a small store, but it is well *stocked*.
The pond is *stocked* with trout every spring.

senses.gloss: Short, solid and strong-looking.
examples: A *stocky* man in a gray coat opened the door.
He is *stocky* like his father.
The *stockier* players get pushed into the line.

contrast: In American English *stodgy* is about people and institutions. British writers also use it for heavy food: *a stodgy pudding*.

senses.gloss: Dull, old-fashioned and much too serious.
examples: The bank has a *stodgy* image it is trying to shake.
He is less *stodgy* than he looks in that suit.
The magazine got *stodgier* after the new editor arrived.

form: from the Stoic philosophers of ancient Greece

senses.gloss: Accepting pain or trouble calmly, without complaining.
examples: She was *stoic* about the whole diagnosis.
He kept a *stoic* silence through the entire meeting.
The crew was *more stoic* about the delay than the passengers.

senses.gloss: Showing almost no emotion and hard to excite or upset.
examples: The guard stood there with a *stolid* expression.
He is a *stolid* man who says maybe twenty words a day.
She stayed *stolid* while everyone around her panicked.

senses.gloss: Completely cold, with no warmth left at all.
examples: My coffee was *stone-cold* by the time I sat down.
The radiators were *stone-cold* all weekend.

senses.gloss: Informal, before a noun or adjective: completely, with no doubt about it.
examples: He was *stone-cold* sober the whole night.
That album is a *stone-cold* classic.

senses.gloss: Informal: high from marijuana.
examples: He was too *stoned* to follow the plot.
Half the audience was *stoned*.
They got *stoned* and ordered three pizzas.

senses.gloss: Covered with or full of stones.
examples: Nothing grows in that *stony* soil.
The path down to the beach is steep and *stony*.
The ground gets *stonier* as you climb.

senses.gloss: Showing no feeling and no friendliness at all.
examples: My question was met with *stony* silence.
She gave him a *stony* look and turned away.

senses.gloss: With the back and shoulders bent permanently forward.
examples: A *stooped* old man shuffled to the counter.
Years at a desk left him *stooped*.
She recognized his *stooped* shoulders from across the street.

position: attributive only — before a noun: *store-bought cookies*
contrast: *Store-bought* is the American word; British English says *shop-bought*.

senses.gloss: Bought ready-made in a store instead of made at home.
examples: She brought *store-bought* cookies and apologized for it.
Use fresh basil, not the *store-bought* sauce.
A *store-bought* crust saves you an hour.

position: attributive only — before a noun: *a storied career*
form: -ed from *story* — full of stories worth telling

senses.gloss: Famous for a long history that people tell stories about.
examples: He ended a *storied* career with one last title.
The Celtics are one of the most *storied* franchises in basketball.
They play in a *storied* old ballpark downtown.

senses.gloss: With strong wind and rain.
examples: It was a *stormy* night and the power went out.
The sea looked *stormy* even from the hotel.
February was the *stormiest* month in years.

senses.gloss: Full of angry argument and strong feeling.
examples: They had a *stormy* marriage that lasted nine years.
The council meeting turned *stormy* after the vote.

senses.gloss: Of a person: rather fat and solid — a gentler word than *fat*.
examples: A *stout* woman in a straw hat was selling tickets.
He has gotten *stouter* since he retired.

senses.gloss: Thick and strong, and not likely to break.
examples: Wear *stout* boots — the trail is rough.
The door is held by a *stout* oak beam.

senses.gloss: Brave and determined, in the face of something hard.
examples: The town put up a *stout* defense of its school.
He remains a *stout* supporter of the program.

contrast: *Straight* is also a very common adverb: *Go straight ahead*, *Come straight home*. And do not confuse it with *strait* (a narrow channel of water).

senses.gloss: Going one way without bending or curving.
examples: Draw a *straight* line from here to the corner.
She has long *straight* hair.
This road is *straighter* than the old one through the hills.

senses.gloss: Level, even, or hanging in the right position.
examples: Is the picture *straight*?
Your tie isn't *straight*.

senses.gloss: Honest and direct, with nothing hidden.
examples: Just give me a *straight* answer.
I'll be *straight* with you: we can't afford it.

senses.gloss: One after another, with no break — always before a noun.
examples: They have won five *straight* games.
It rained for ten *straight* days.

senses.gloss: Of a strong drink: with nothing added.
examples: He drinks his whiskey *straight*.
I'll take a *straight* bourbon, no ice.

senses.gloss: Easy to do or understand, with no hidden complications.
examples: The application process is pretty *straightforward*.
It should be a *straightforward* repair.
Her explanation was *more straightforward* than anything in the manual.

senses.gloss: Of a person: honest and saying plainly what they think.
examples: He is *straightforward* about what he wants.
I like her *straightforward* way of dealing with people.

senses.gloss: Of a relationship or atmosphere: tense and close to breaking.
examples: Relations between the two countries are *strained*.
Dinner was polite but *strained*.

senses.gloss: Of a smile, voice or look: forced, not natural.
examples: She answered with a *strained* smile.
His voice sounded *strained* on the phone.

senses.gloss: Of a muscle: hurt by being stretched too far.
examples: He is out for two weeks with a *strained* hamstring.
Ice a *strained* muscle for the first day.

contrast: The first part is *strait* (narrow, tight), not *straight*. Also written *strait-laced*.

senses.gloss: Having very strict, old-fashioned ideas about how people should behave.
examples: Her parents were *straitlaced* and hated the whole idea.
It is a *straitlaced* little town with no bars.
He is less *straitlaced* than he pretends to be.

senses.gloss: Left in a place with no way to get away from it.
examples: The storm left hundreds of travelers *stranded* at the airport.
We were *stranded* on the side of the highway for two hours.
A *stranded* whale was pushed back out with the tide.

senses.gloss: Of a dress or top: made with no straps over the shoulders.
examples: She wore a *strapless* black dress.
The gown is *strapless*, so bring a wrap.
*Strapless* tops are hard to keep in place.

position: attributive only — before a noun: *a strapping young man*

senses.gloss: Of a young person: tall, strong and healthy-looking.
examples: Her son is a *strapping* eighteen-year-old now.
Two *strapping* farmhands carried the beam by themselves.
He grew into a *strapping* kid who could lift anything.

senses.gloss: Done as part of a long-term plan to reach an important goal.
examples: The hire was a *strategic* move, not a favor.
We need to be *more strategic* about where we spend the money.

senses.gloss: Military: important for winning a war or holding a position.
examples: The bridge has *strategic* value for both sides.
The treaty limits *strategic* weapons.

senses.gloss: Arranged in clear layers, one on top of another.
examples: The cliff shows *stratified* bands of red rock.
The lake is *stratified* in summer, with warm water on top.

senses.gloss: Of a society: divided into sharply separated classes.
examples: It was a rigidly *stratified* society.
The city is *more stratified* by income than it was in 1980.

position: attributive only — before a noun: *a stray dog*
contrast: *A stray* is also a noun for a lost animal: *She took in a stray*.

senses.gloss: Of an animal: lost, or living on the street with no owner.
examples: A *stray* cat has been sleeping on our porch.
The shelter is full of *stray* dogs.

senses.gloss: Separated from the rest, or there only by accident.
examples: A *stray* bullet went through the window.
She tucked a *stray* hair behind her ear.

position: both — before a noun in the internet sense

senses.gloss: Sent over the internet in a continuous flow, so you watch or listen as it arrives.
examples: We pay for three *streaming* services and watch one.
The concert is available as a *streaming* video.
Most of their money now comes from *streaming* revenue.

senses.gloss: Flowing or pouring steadily.
examples: She came in with her eyes *streaming*.
The windows were *streaming* with rain.

senses.gloss: Shaped smoothly so that air or water flows past it easily.
examples: The new train has a *streamlined* nose.
Dolphins have a perfectly *streamlined* body.

senses.gloss: Made simpler and faster by cutting out unnecessary steps.
examples: The application is *streamlined* — it takes ten minutes now.
They want a *more streamlined* approval process.

contrast: Before a noun it usually takes a hyphen: *a street-smart kid*, but *she is street smart*.

senses.gloss: Good at handling the dangers and tricks of life in a city.
examples: He is *street smart* in a way you cannot learn in school.
She was sixteen and already *street smart*.
You need someone *more street smart* than an intern for that job.

senses.gloss: Experienced enough to look after yourself in a rough part of a city.
examples: The kids on that block are *streetwise* by ten.
He plays a *streetwise* detective who breaks every rule.
She is *streetwise* enough not to walk there alone.

senses.gloss: Needing a lot of physical effort and energy.
examples: Avoid *strenuous* exercise for a week after the surgery.
The hike is long but not *strenuous*.

senses.gloss: Of effort or opposition: energetic and determined.
examples: The bill passed over the *strenuous* objections of the mayor.
They made *strenuous* efforts to find the owner.

contrast: The person is *stressed*; the thing that does it is *stressful*: *a stressful week leaves you stressed*.

senses.gloss: Worried and tense because of too much pressure.
examples: She has been *stressed* about the move for weeks.
Everyone is *stressed* out by the deadline.
He looked *more stressed* than I had ever seen him.

senses.gloss: Of a syllable: said with more force than the ones around it.
examples: In *record* the noun, the first syllable is *stressed*.
Mark the *stressed* syllable in each word.

contrast: *stressful* describes the situation, *stressed* the person: *a stressful job*, *a stressed employee*.

senses.gloss: Causing worry and pressure.
examples: Moving is one of the most *stressful* things you can do.
It was a *stressful* week at work.
Flying with a toddler is *more stressful* than any meeting.

senses.gloss: Pulled out so it is longer, wider or tighter than before.
examples: The canvas is *stretched* over a wooden frame.
The collar is *stretched* out of shape.

senses.gloss: Of money, staff or time: barely enough for what has to be done.
examples: The department is *stretched* thin this month.
Our budget is *more stretched* than it was last year.

senses.gloss: Able to stretch easily and go back to its shape.
examples: These pants are *stretchy* and comfortable.
Look for a *stretchy* fabric with some spandex in it.
The gray ones are *stretchier* than the black.

position: both — often right after the noun: *a town stricken by drought*
form: an old past participle of *strike*; also the second half of compounds — *grief-stricken*, *panic-stricken*

senses.gloss: Badly hit by illness, grief or some other trouble.
examples: He was *stricken* with pneumonia in his last year.
Aid reached the *stricken* villages after three days.
She sat there *stricken*, unable to say a word.

senses.gloss: Demanding that rules be obeyed, and not forgiving when they are not.
examples: My parents were *strict* about bedtime.
She is *strict* with her students but they love her.
The new principal is much *stricter* than the old one.

senses.gloss: Of a rule, order or meaning: exact, and to be followed exactly.
examples: He gave us *strict* instructions not to open it.
In the *strict* sense of the word, it isn't a fruit.

senses.gloss: Loud and harsh, in a way that hurts the ear.
examples: A *strident* alarm went off down the hall.
Her voice got *strident* when she was tired.

senses.gloss: Expressing an opinion so forcefully that it puts people off.
examples: The paper has taken a *more strident* tone since the election.
He is one of the *most strident* critics of the plan.

senses.gloss: So unusual or clear that you notice it right away.
examples: There is a *striking* difference between the two drafts.
The *most striking* thing about the house is the light.
The similarity is *striking*.

senses.gloss: Attractive in a bold, unusual way.
examples: She is a *striking* woman with silver hair.
The building is *striking* from every angle.

senses.gloss: Of rules or standards: strict, detailed and hard to meet.
examples: California has *stringent* emissions rules.
The lab follows *stringent* safety procedures.
Banks face *more stringent* requirements than they did in 2007.

senses.gloss: Of food: full of tough fibers that are hard to chew.
examples: The beef was dry and *stringy*.
Old celery gets *stringier* the longer you keep it.

senses.gloss: Of hair: thin, greasy and hanging in separate pieces.
examples: His hair was long and *stringy*.
She pushed her wet, *stringy* bangs off her forehead.

contrast: One syllable, rhyming with *wiped* — not *STRY-pid*.

senses.gloss: Having stripes.
examples: He wore a blue *striped* shirt.
The awning is *striped* green and white.
She picked the *striped* wallpaper for the hallway.

position: attributive only — before a noun: *a stripped-down version*

senses.gloss: With everything extra taken away, leaving only the basics.
examples: The free plan is a *stripped-down* version of the app.
They played a *stripped-down* set with two guitars.
He bought the *stripped-down* model with no navigation.

ru: сильный; прочный; крепкий (о вкусе, напитке); твёрдый

senses.gloss: Having a lot of physical power.
examples: You have to be *strong* to carry that up the stairs.
She is the *strongest* swimmer on the team.
He is *stronger* now than he was before the injury.

senses.gloss: Well made and not easily broken or damaged.
examples: Use a *strong* box for the books.
The bridge is *strong* enough for trucks.

senses.gloss: Of a taste, smell or drink: intense, with a lot of flavor or alcohol.
examples: I like my coffee *strong*.
There was a *strong* smell of gas in the kitchen.

senses.gloss: Firmly felt or hard to argue with.
examples: She has *strong* opinions about the schools.
There is *strong* evidence that the drug works.

position: attributive only — before a noun: *strong-arm tactics*
contrast: It is also a verb: *they strong-armed him into signing*.

senses.gloss: Using force or heavy pressure to get what you want.
examples: The union accused management of *strong-arm* tactics.
He built the company with *strong-arm* methods nobody talks about.
They used *strong-arm* pressure on the smaller suppliers.

senses.gloss: Having firm opinions and not easily talked out of them.
examples: She is *strong-minded* and says exactly what she thinks.
It takes a *strong-minded* judge to rule against her own party.
The committee needs someone *more strong-minded* than him.

senses.gloss: Determined to do what you want, even when people push back.
examples: Their youngest is *strong-willed* and will not be rushed.
You need to be *strong-willed* to finish a program like that.
He is the *most strong-willed* person I know.

senses.gloss: Having to do with the frame that holds a building up.
examples: The inspector found no *structural* damage.
That wall is *structural*, so you cannot just take it out.

senses.gloss: Built into the way a system is organized, not caused by one event.
examples: The deficit is *structural*, not a one-year problem.
They are looking at *structural* changes to the whole department.
